summary: Records the MPLS Working Group's consensus to focus on RSVP-TE, from RFC 3209, as the signaling protocol for traffic engineering, and not to start new work on constraint-based LDP from RFC 3212.

plainLanguage.summary: Two competing ways of setting up network paths existed. The working group chose one to keep working on and stopped working on the other.

subtitle: The MPLS working group picks RSVP-TE over CR-LDP as the way to signal traffic-engineered paths.

tldr.problem: Two competing protocols, RSVP-TE and CR-LDP, had both reached Proposed Standard for setting up constraint-based label switched paths, which duplicated work across several IETF working groups.
tldr.mechanism: The MPLS working group agreed to focus on RSVP-TE (RFC 3209) for traffic engineering signaling and to take on no new work on CR-LDP (RFC 3212), while leaving CR-LDP's document status unchanged.
tldr.outcome: The recommendations were accepted by the IESG. CR-LDP stays referenceable at Proposed Standard but is not advanced further, and individual contributions about it are discouraged.

today: RFC 3468 is Informational and, according to the unit metadata, updates RFC 3212, RFC 3472, RFC 3475 and RFC 3476. It has not been obsoleted. It records the decision that RSVP-TE is the focus for MPLS traffic engineering signaling.

sections.title: What the Document Records
sections.content:
RFC 3468 is not a protocol specification. It documents a decision of the Multiprotocol Label Switching (MPLS) Working Group: to keep developing RFC 3209 (RSVP-TE) as the signaling protocol for MPLS traffic engineering, and to start no new work on RFC 3212 (Constraint-Based LSP Setup using LDP, called CR-LDP).

Section 6 holds the actual recommendations, and the document says the IESG accepted them. All other sections describe how the consensus was reached. No other action is taken on the status of RFC 3212 or of the RFCs that extend it.
sections.plainLanguage: This paper is a record of a vote. It says which of two tools a team will keep working on, and explains how they decided.

sections.title: Two Tracks for One Job
sections.content:
Very early in MPLS standardization, in 1997, it was clear that providers would need a protocol to set up label switched paths (LSPs) that take other information, such as quality-of-service parameters, into account. Work went down two tracks: extensions to RSVP for MPLS tunnels (RFC 3209) and extensions to LDP for constraint-based LSPs (RFC 3212).

Each choice looked reasonable. RSVP already handled QoS information and resource reservation in an IP environment, so only label distribution had to be added. LDP was designed for label distribution, so adding extra TLVs for QoS information was not revolutionary either. The working group never reached consensus on one way, and both protocols were progressed to Proposed Standard.
sections.plainLanguage: Two teams each made a different tool for the same chore. Both tools worked, so nobody could agree which one to use.

sections.title: How the Decision Was Reached
sections.content:
A June 2002 survey of GMPLS implementations had 22 responding implementers. Twenty-one of the 22 included GMPLS signaling based on RFC 3209, and only 3 included signaling based on RFC 3212. That prompted the question of whether two protocols for the same thing made sense, and the working group took it up at its July 2002 meeting in Yokohama before moving it to the mailing lists.

The first proposal was to make CR-LDP Informational and keep only RSVP-TE on the standards track. The response was largely positive, but two problems were raised: non-IETF standards reference RFC 3212, and RFC 2026 documents no process for moving a standards track document to a non-standards-track status. The RFC concludes that, together, these made the original proposal not viable, while support for further standards track development of CR-LDP was extremely small.

The question was then reformulated: focus on RSVP-TE and discontinue the working group effort on CR-LDP, with no change to CR-LDP's document status. The RFC adds that it is meant to discourage, though not prohibit, continued CR-LDP work. Close to 90% of the people taking part said they supported or at least accepted this outcome.

The RFC notes the IETF process had no description of moving a standards track RFC to a non-standards-track status, nor a ban on it, and it cites RFCs 2673 and 2874 as earlier cases moved from Proposed Standard to Experimental.
sections.plainLanguage: First they wanted to demote one tool, but other people already depended on it. So they chose a gentler plan: keep it on the shelf, but stop making new parts for it.

sections.title: The Consensus and the Recommendation
sections.content:
The working group chairs stated consensus on these points:

  • The group focuses on RSVP-TE (RFC 3209) for traffic engineering signaling.
  • It undertakes no new work on CR-LDP, takes on no new working group documents about it, and entertains no efforts to promote it beyond Proposed Standard.
  • RFC 3212, RFC 3213 and RFC 3214 remain Proposed Standard.
  • Eight existing CR-LDP related working group drafts are still taken through the process to Proposed Standard or Informational.
  • Individual CR-LDP contributions are discouraged, not prohibited, and the charter is updated.
  • Relevant standards organizations are notified of the change of focus.

Section 6 asks the IESG to confirm the decision, to adopt as IETF policy not to entertain work that advances RFC 3212 or related RFCs beyond Proposed Standard or new working group extensions to it, to review the process for moving documents off the standards track, and to publish the document as an Informational RFC.
sections.plainLanguage: They agreed to keep the old tool where people can find it, finish the parts already half built, and not start anything new for it.

sections.title: Security and IANA Considerations
sections.content: The document only discusses a refocusing of the MPLS Working Group's work, so it states that it brings no new security considerations. It likewise brings no IANA considerations.
sections.plainLanguage: Nothing about how safe the tools are changed. Only the plan for who works on what changed.
